title: Columba on Iona
hookLine: an Irish monk exiled to an island founds a mission that reaches Scotland

cards: A gray bird drops out of the sky onto a beach. It's a crane, worn out from a long flight over the sea, too tired to move. Somebody saw this coming.
A few days before, the abbot of the island told one of his monks: go down to the western shore and watch. A crane will come from Ireland, blown off course and exhausted.
Carry it to a house nearby, feed it, look after it for three days. Then it will fly home. And it does.
The abbot who sent him had come from Ireland too, and made this island his home. His name was Columba.

teach.h: WHY HE LEFT: THE SOURCES DIFFER.
teach.b: The crane story comes from Adomnán, a later abbot of the same island, who wrote a life of Columba. In Adomnán's telling, Columba blesses the bird because it came from the land of their fathers. Why did Columba leave?

Adomnán says simply that he sailed from Ireland wishing to be a pilgrim for Christ. Later tradition tells a sharper story, of a quarrel and a battle, and an exile laid on him as penance. The old sources don't settle it.
He came to a small island off the west coast of what is now Scotland, called Iona, and with his companions built a monastery there.

Bede, the English monk and historian, writes that Columba came to preach the word of God to the northern Picts, and that the island was given to him for a monastery. From that small place, monks went out.
Bede tells how one of them, Aidan, went from Iona to the English king Oswald in Northumbria, and set up a monastery on another island, Lindisfarne.
So a monk who left home became the start of a long chain of homes for others.

Adomnán's Latin for what Columba wanted is peregrinatio, pilgrimage. Some readers hear in it more than a trip with a return ticket: leaving home for Christ and not coming back, an exile chosen and offered.
In Columba's last days, Adomnán says, a white horse came and laid its head against him and wept. The horse, he says, knew its master was leaving.

how: Christians in Scotland and Ireland remember Saint Columba, also called Colum Cille, and Iona still draws pilgrims and an ecumenical community that keeps a daily rhythm of prayer there.

s: the old sources agree on why Columba left Ireland
Adomnán says he went as a pilgrim for Christ. the story of a battle and a penance is later tradition.
Bede says the island was given to Columba for a monastery
and that he came to preach to the northern Picts.
in the crane story, Columba keeps the bird on Iona
the monk looks after it for three days, and it flies back toward Ireland.

games.q: you're the monk sent to the western shore. an exhausted crane from Ireland lands at your feet. what do you do?
o: carry it in and look after it for three days.
leave it. it's only a bird.
keep it on the island for good.
games.why: he does what Columba told him: feeds it, shelters it, and on the third day it flies home. the abbot who sent him had made the island his home.

practice: Find a quiet place: a parked car, a back step, or just close your eyes where you are.

Let the noise of the day be the sea around the island, still there but out past the shore, and notice one thing that came to you from far away today, the way the crane came: a message, a memory, a worry.
Look after it for a minute, and if you pray, hand it to God.
